utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Theresa McHenry appearing for the Prosecution along with Mr. Turone. Mr. Niemann is in another courtroom at the present time but will at some point today, I assume, be joining us. Also, we have a new case manager. Ms. Udo had a conflict, and so now Mr. George Huber is also with us for the Prosecution as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Welcome to the team. May we have the Defence appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Zejnil Delalic is also co-defended by my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Tomislav Kuzmanovic for defendant Zdravko Mucic. Mr. Olujic will not be here this week. He will rejoin us on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey here for Mr. Esad Landzo along with co-counsel Ms. Nancy Boler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before the witnesses are called, I think it is necessary for me to point out what Ms. Residovic has sent in to us. In her reply to a status conference, an earlier list of witnesses was filed numbering about 30. Subsequent to that, I have now this morning received another list of witnesses not departing from that, and I have not counted them, but I think it has not made any material difference to what was submitted. The document which has just presented these witnesses shows that this list includes the witnesses scheduled to testify from today to the 29th of May. I'm hoping that the estimation of the duration of the Defence case, that is the Defence of the first accused, is likely to continue to the end of June. This is the projection. Actually, I thought during the status conference and subsequent observations, it was understood that the Trial Chamber will not accept repetitions or duplications or further evidence on areas subsequently traversed by the Defence earlier witnesses. We thought that it is a waste of time. It will go over old ground and it does not explain the issues for them. We don't see why the Trial Chamber should interest itself in duplicating its witnesses. Now, I should not be regarded as being unfair or rude on pointing out to counsel the charges which they are obliged to defend. Please let me read what the Prosecution in its charges has stated. If you look at the indictment at paragraph 13, it states: "All of the victims referred to in the charges contained in this indictment were at all relevant times detainees in Celebici camp and were persons protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949." And 14: "All acts described in the paragraphs below occurred in the Celebici camp in the Konjic municipality." I think nothing can be clearer than this. Then it went on in paragraph 15 to say: "The allegations contained in paragraphs seven through fourteen are re-alleged and incorporated into each of the relevant charges set out below." As I said, paragraph 14 states: "All acts described in the paragraphs below occurred in the Celebici camp in the Konjic municipality." This is what it says. Now, when you read the witnesses and what they intend to say, you find that almost a significant number of them relate to role and responsibility of the coordinator and TG-1 commander. This is merely what it says. You will find that it talks about role and responsibility in respect of Jablanica municipality, not minding what the Prosecution has stated, what concerns them are things which happened in Konjic municipality. To find so many, about two of the witnesses talking about Jablanica and then Hadzici municipality, then Prozor municipality, and then it goes to general principles which have been very clearly stated by both Hadzihuseinovic and by Cerovac, all of them who are Defence witnesses themselves. Now, defence structures in Konjic municipality have been very clearly stated by the chief of staff of the municipality. When we talk about conditions in Konjic municipality, that has also been clearly stated. We have had so many of them. I suppose the more that is said, we are so daft that we should be told so many times so that we can understand what is being said, when both the Defence and the Prosecution are saying the same thing. We have heard it so many times that a coordinator has no military responsibility. On both sides they have emphasised that. Why then do we go forward to continue to talk about his position? Now, again we're talking about hearing about the liberation of Bradina. There was no one at that who was charged both as coordinator and TG-1 commander. He was neither at the time that Bradina was liberated, so how does it come in? I don't know. Now, there are areas where perhaps one might make a concession. An officer like Mustafa Polutak, who himself was sometime commander of TG-1. Obviously, one expects he should be called to say what happened, his position, his relationship, one expects that. Perhaps there might be the question of a MUP operation and the like who perhaps I would expect, but all the others are completely irrelevant and a waste of time, money and patience on the part of everybody concerned. I'm surprised that it happens. Now, for conditions in Celebici, why do we have to get in as many witnesses as this? How come so many? I'm still not too satisfied about the motives for this type of multiplication of witnesses. There must be other motives other than clarity of the evidence intended to be tendered to the Trial Chamber. I'm not satisfied at all, whatsoever, because the witnesses which are lined up today I do not know, but if I follow this list, it appears that Agic Saban Witness D, Saban is about role and responsibility of coordinator, joint command. We have heard enough of that Operation Oganj. Then the witness of the defence structures in Konjic, well, we have heard enough from the chief of Celebici. We have heard about the role and responsibility of coordinator, liberation of Bradina. I think they are completely irrelevant to what we intend to hear now. Perhaps you would say I have not heard the witnesses so I do not know exactly what they want to say. I'm only forewarning, if you want to call them, you might still call them, but I'm entitled to stop irrelevancies being introduced into evidence or repetition of what has been said here in the interests of justice of this case. This is what I intend to tell you. So if you want to, you can still proceed, but I reserve the right to tell you what the Trial Chamber will have. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the status conference, what we did is, we deleted 12 witnesses from the witness list which had been previously submitted, taking into account that the issues that they were to speak to have been sufficiently clarified by other witnesses. In the letter which was submitted today, we said that we would re-evaluate each witness that is to come and that we will continue to reduce the number of witnesses. We believe that we will finish our witnesses in the week following the week which will be the break for us. This is after long and arduous work that we have done. Now, I want to turn to the counts. Here we have, for instance, count 3 which he is charged with being responsible for the Celebici camp in the position of superiority. Further, it is said that all guards who entered the camp and who mistreated prisoners there were under the command of Mr. Delalic and that he was aware that he did nothing to stop. We're looking at point 3 and point 7. Further on, there's also inhumane mistreatment. They are all based, founded on what actually was happening at Celebici but also are based on what the position of responsibility of the coordinator and the commander of the Tactical Group had. If today we agree with the Prosecutor that the coordinator was not a military position, if we can agree on that, the Defence will not ask any more questions in that regard and can dismiss any witness that would speak to that. We are not sure that we have not clarified enough the position of the commander of the Tactical Group. We have not yet called enough witnesses who could speak to that, but the burden of proof lies with the Prosecutor. The document of 27 July which calls him the commander of all armed forces in the territory of several municipalities, we then need to call a witness to speak whether Mr. Delalic was commander in Jablanica, Prozor, Igman, et cetera, so that we can prove that Mr. Delalic was not in Celebici, that he did not enter the prison. If the Prosecution agrees that Mr. Delalic did not have responsibility of that kind, then we can also now stipulate that he was not responsible for these acts committed in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have finished? Please proceed to call your witnesses. I have told you the principles under which the Trial Chamber receives evidence. First, it has to be relevant; secondly, it must be related to the charges before the Trial Chamber. If you decide to introduce evidence which is irrelevant, duplicating, then we have the right to reject them and, therefore, it must have been wasted both on the part of the registry which paid for the witness to come and on the Trial Chamber which had the duty, and sometimes a painful duty, of listening to irrelevant evidence. You can go ahead. Call your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already told the Prosecutor the witness who was slated to come on first has taken ill and so we want to call two witnesses, Enver Redzepovic and Zihad Salihamidzic. This would be out of order and we beg for your indulgence on this because -- and I'm sorry my colleague is trying to say something. Your Honours, I call Mr. Enver Redzepovic as the next Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just to advise Your Honours, Ms. Residovic did tell us a few minutes ago that the witness that had been scheduled for today had a headache and that she would be calling another witness. The witness that she is now calling is the witness that was supposed to testify last this week. She has also given us some documents a few minutes ago that we have never seen before. For that reason, we have no objection and want to hurry things along, we have no objection to her calling him at the present time, but we will be requesting that cross-examination be postponed until, at least, tomorrow morning since we only found out a few minutes ago and haven't had a chance to look at the documents, much less even be prepared for the witness. We can, of course, go on with the direct testimony of the second witness, but under these conditions, we think it would be unfair to make us cross-examine when we are entirely unprepared. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it the same gentleman who was the TO commander on the 18th of April when he retired and was replaced by Esad Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was the first commander of the new Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- assembly and he was to retire. And then the assembly recommended that Esad Ramic be appointed as a commander. Is it the same gentleman? So what can he tell us?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the first commander. Only one person was the first commander of the new Territorial Defence and through this witness, we will prove that, that the Territorial Defence started functioning according to the new regulations, something that the Prosecution was questioning. Following him, Mr. Esad Ramic was appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you want to postpone his cross-examination? He's not a commander at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not the commander at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously, I don't know exactly what he's going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I think the chief of staff has said sufficient about the situation at the time. Call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat. Take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court. Good morning, sir. Good morning. Will you please introduce yourself to the court by giving us your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Enver Redzepovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, before I proceed with questions, let me draw your attention to the fact that our conversation needs to be interpreted, so wait until the interpretation of my question into English has been completed and answer that question only then. In that way, the questions and answers will be entered in the transcript and everyone present in the courtroom will be able to follow what we are saying. Have you understood what I have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On these headphones?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you will be able to hear the sound of the interpretation on those headphones. If necessary, you can turn on the volume. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Redzepovic, will you tell us, please, where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of May, 1955, in Zemun, the present day Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your training and education and your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to primary and secondary school, I graduated from the military academy, which I attended from 1974 until 1978, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you, Mr. Redzepovic, at the beginning of April, 1992, when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if we consider the relevant date to be April the 6th, at the time, I was on duty as an officer in the operations training department of the TO staff in Konjic. Which means, I was employed in the TO staff of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your superior commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I started working there, and that was in September, 1991, the commander was Ahmed Boric until November, 1991. And as of November '91, Smajo Prevljak became the commander until April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did a reorganisation of the TO occur sometime in April, 1992, so that it became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a reorganisation. In view of the fact that the former republic had been promoted and recognised by the international community, it had the duty to form its own armed forces, so that on the 8th of April, the presidency, at its meeting, transformed the republic staff, which was subordinated to the SSNO in Belgrade, the federal secretariat for national defence, and it was promoted to become the staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, the Trial Chamber has already heard about that from expert witnesses. My question is, in accordance with those regulations, was the Territorial Defence in Konjic reorganised and what is the substance of that reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no real substantive changes, but it was only the system of control and command that was reorganised. The units and the command remain the same. The tasks, duties, obligations of individuals, and groups more or less remained the same. But in the system of control and command, some changes occurred in the sense that we were no longer responsible and accountable to the regime in Belgrade, but rather to the structure of government inside as well as to the military authority there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Redzepovic, who was the municipal staff subordinated to, from that day on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal staff, according to an earlier instructions on organisation, and as stipulated by the constitution and other military regulation, it was subordinated to the district staff in Mostar. Since the Mostar district staff was not operating, due to well-known reasons, that is the occupying force was present there with its military strength, we were subordinated to the TO staff to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, were you appointed commander of this new reorganised Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. The assembly, of the municipal assembly of Konjic, at its regular session on the 17th of April, proposed me to be nominated and within a period of three the five days, the ministry and the TO staff actually appointed me commander of the municipal staff of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, from the time when you were appointed until the end of '92, when the fourth corps was formed, the competence of the municipality, was it limited to the nomination of commanders, whereas the republican staff had the duty to actually make the appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told the court that the municipality agreed to propose you to that post, whereas the actual appointment was carried out by the Republican staff, was that the established practice that remained in effect until the formation of the fourth corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to numerous unfavourable circumstances, within which we waged the defensive war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was the practice that remained in effect until the corps was formed in the region of Herzegovina, that is the fourth corps. After that, the fourth corps appointed commanders for its zones of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you became commander of the municipal staff, tell me, Mr. Redzepovic, were there any Green Berets or the Patriotic League in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no Green Berets, nor a Patriotic League. And I hadn't heard about them, nor did I have any occasion to meet any member of the Green Berets or the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, during the time you were commander in Konjic Municipality, was a general mobilisation proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A general mobilisation was proclaimed at the level of the Republic in June, in June, as far as I can recall. But instructions on the organisation and use of TO staffs, drafted by the ministry of defence and TO staff and which was forwarded to us, and on the basis of which we acted, gave us the opportunity to carry out a mobilisation even before the mobilisation was officially proclaimed at the level of the Republic, which we in fact did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me to what kind of units, defensive units, were people mobilised to, after the mobilisation was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we proclaimed the mobilisation, we encountered a large number of problems. One of them was that people, members of our units of Serb ethnic origin, boycotted the mobilisation and refused to join the Territorial Defence forces formed by the legal state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A second problem was that in the course of the mobilisation, we were unable to distribute arms, ammunition, equipment and everything else that any soldier should have, soldier and officer immediately, and this was one of the greatest problems we had, both at the beginning and later on during the war. And a series of other problems, which I need not list, but these were the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining this. Mr. Redzepovic, tell us, as a commander, did you try to deal with the problems with the Serb population in a peaceful manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. If the persons who held various positions testify here, truthfully and frankly, they will confirm that we did our best to preserve the multi ethnic population and to organise them to defend the territory of Konjic Municipality. Those efforts, however, were fruitless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who constituted the defensive forces of Konjic Municipality while you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my term of office, we had within our defensive forces, units and the TO staff and the Croatian Defence Council. Those were the military forces, plus, among the police forces, the MUP which was there within the territory of Konjic Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, while you were the commander, did a representative of the Republican staff come to Konjic to assist you in organising the defence under these unexpected wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. A man came from the republic staff, his name was Dzambasevic, Asim Dzambasevic, and this was probably a reaction to our request while the communications were still functional, we asked the Republic staff to help us in the practical organisation and in finding our way around in view of the unexpected nature of the tasks confronting us. In the second half of April, Mr. Dzambasevic came to our staff, to our headquarters, and his assistance was invaluable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did attacks and killings start while you were still commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And the first attacks were carried out in the region of Ljubljana, where two of our members were killed, one was from the TO staff and the other from the HVO. Our member was -- our member's name was Alic and the HVO's member name was Azinovic and this occurred somewhere around the 20th of April. Using small arms, these two men were killed and the first attacks on Konjic, the first artillery attacks, were carried out at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a witness of the fact that the authorities in Konjic sought to act in accordance with the regulations and to protect the whole population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am. I am a witness and I claim that all the bodies, both civilian and military worked and did their best to work in line with the rules and regulations, which also exist for the circumstances of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that one of the elements of the defensive forces was the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, will you please tell me whether the HVO was a well-organised structure in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why are you going into that field again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please ask the next question. Go into another field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did you personally need permission from the HVO to be able to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And the procedure was as follows --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is not necessary, Mr. Redzepovic, you need not explain to us the procedure because the Trial Chamber is already aware of that. Is it true that upon arrival to The Hague, you gave me a copy of the permit on the basis of which you were able to leave the town? If you did, I should like to show you that permit, so that we can see what you needed to leave the town. Can it be marked for identification, please, and shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the permit and it is only with this permit that I was able to leave Konjic. For which I needed a permit of this particular kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a document which is illustrative of certain competencies in the Town of Konjic and is relevant from the standpoint of responsibility, the witness has identified it and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whose responsibility is it meant for?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The responsibility for allowing people to leave the town was with the HVO, one of the defence forces of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There's nothing in this about HVO's responsibility. If you are saying that someone needed a permit to travel outside, I can understand, it does not go to the responsibility of anyone who is involved in this litigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the prosecution has produced some evidence of the international monitoring commission about the split authority over Celebici, so you may get a more complete picture on who controlled which segment of the authority in the area. For instance, the prosecution has offered through their expert evidence, some evidence in that regard, so now we can further elucidate the HVO role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have no intention of interrupting your train of thought. When you are saying that this illustrates responsibility, you should now show whose responsibility it was, not this witness. In fact, it restricted his movements, unless he had this. That is what you are saying. And if he hadn't this permit, he had no right to move. So it's not a matter of his responsibility. And the competence does not lay in his own evidence, so why do you bring it in, in order to show that his movement was restricted because of the authority exercised by some other persons? This is all you need to do, but not of what responsibility you are trying to bring into it. As I have always said, one should understand the case you are presenting and present it properly. While I pass it or not, I did not know you are making so many errors, I just leave you to carry on. We'll admit it as a permit enabling him to travel outside the city, that's all, not that it showed any responsibility on his part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit D 176/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, at the time when you were commander, did the Territorial Defence have, at that time, its own military police and if it did not, who did they rely on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when I was a commander, the Territorial Defence did not have its own military police. And the police and security affairs were handled, and which we needed, by the official MUP. And it was the HVO that had a special police unit. And this is how we solved the problem of the military police. We went to the HVO and their police force. And it was staffed by both Croats and Muslims, so it was mixed, and this is why we trusted and had confidence in this police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, while you were commander of the TO headquarters, were certain military facilities, in the territorial Konjic Municipality, come under your control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first military facility, which we as an army, that is a Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, placed under our control, was a military plant, Igman. This was a plant which produced ordnance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the other facility, the next facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other military facility was the Celebici warehouse, where certain amount of materiel was being stored and, in principle, this was only a warehouse, a depot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, can you say who took part in taking control -- taking over the Celebici barracks from the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both in taking over the Celebici depot and the Igman plant were the Territorial Defence and the MUP of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these facilities taken over without use of force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the process of taking control of these facilities, no force was used, physical, military or otherwise. All the facilities were taken over by agreement and in accordance with requests by both civilian and military leadership which were appropriate for the extraordinary circumstances in which we had found ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, do you know where the weapons which were found in the Celebici barracks were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have evidence on that. We already have evidence on that, that they were taken to a farm and a house belonging to a sister of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Why do you want to cover the same field?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honours, that we are revisiting the same issue, but those are relevant facts and we believe that it may be useful to hear them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are rehearing the same evidence. Repetition doesn't make a fact true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is still some controversy there because the Prosecution claims that Zejnil Delalic took over the control of Celebici and turned it into a prison and this is a relevant fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A document was recovered from Inda-Bau where it was said that Mr. Zejnil Delalic wrote in his own handwriting, "I liberated Celebici and I was responsible for the camp and my own brothers being detained." The Prosecution is relying upon that. The evidence is there that Cerovac told us that he was part of the operation that took over Celebici and that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You already have evidence from Cerovac on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you agree too that this is a crucial fact. If there is a witness who can reconfirm the fact, it is repeated, but it does not lose any relevance. I think that it continues to be extremely relevant to your eventual judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was a state prison, Celebici. It wasn't a private prison of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. The prison must have been set up by state authority. Your case is that Zejnil Delalic did not occupy, as a coordinator, any position of authority. He did not occupy any position, as TG commander, in setting up the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Try and go over the evidence of Hadzihuseinovic, the president of the municipal assembly. He gave a lot of evidence as to how the Celebici barracks was handed over to them. His evidence is very clear, so I don't see what that has to do by leading any of the evidence, except even if this witness is saying that he was a member of the team which liberated it, which took it over, it would not be strong enough over what the president has stated and stated very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was commander of the municipal headquarters, and the credibility of every statement and its forcefulness sometimes can be reconfirmed from another angle, from another person who was personally involved. I think that all this will assist you in evaluating the Prosecution's allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He stated how the officer in charge of that place came to him to discuss how he could peacefully hand it over, and it is a peaceful hand-over that this witness is telling us. What difference does it make to what has already been given in evidence? Cerovac also has given evidence on the same thing, two crucial witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Cerovac also took part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You say, Your Honours, that this is a fact, that this has been confirmed without any dispute how these barracks were taken over. If that is what you're saying, I'm not going to ask any questions of this witness, but what the Defence has to also take into account are all these Inda-Bau documents, and we need to clarify these issues as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did the commander of the municipal defence headquarters change in late April and early May? In other words, did you step down from that position and who took over for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since at the time when I had taken over this duty, there were no other better qualified persons, and I was the person who had the most organisational skills and who was the most appropriate person. In my training, I focused on anti-aircraft defence. This was the focus of my work throughout my career. During the period when I was a commander, Mr. Esad Ramic volunteered. He had the same rank. He was a captain and his speciality was ground combat. He was a better qualified person so he replaced me as the commander in late April, in fact, it was on May 1, whereas I took over the duties of the anti-aircraft defences, which is my own speciality, as a commissioned officer, within the organisation of combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, do you know how Mr. Ramic was appointed? Was he proposed by the war presidency and appointed by the headquarters or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have heard enough of how it was done, how Esad Ramic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done in the same way as with myself

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are coming back to the same problem. I note that I was warned by Judge Jan during the testimony of General Pasalic. We are relying on all that, but that seemed to not have been enough for your decision. So we have to keep coming back to this because you have turned down our motion of no case, so if we thought that you had issues you wanted us to call a defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that your contention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you read the proceedings of the assembly, the assembly had appointed Esad Ramic, but your case is it is merely a nomination, it is not an appointment. Before this witness came in, I said we heard in this proceeding that this gentleman was the commanding officer of the TO, then the reasons given in assembly proceeding that he was to retire. And Hadzihuseinovic was the president who was asked a few questions about that also.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but this is the first witness who testified to Esad Ramic being appointed in the same way which means that he was proposed by the war presidency and he was appointed by the republican staff, so he's the first one who is confirming that. This is what the witness just testified to, he was present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has said why Esad Ramic was appointed and he was not allowed to continue. He has given his qualifications. He has given the qualifications of Esad Ramic. He has not said anything from where his appointment came and from where the appointment of Esad Ramic came. He has been talking about his qualifications and the qualifications of Esad Ramic. That's what he was talking about, which we are not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did you say, and if you did, please repeat it, how was Mr. Esad Ramic appointed? I heard your answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please indicate how he was appointed. Ask the witness how Esad Ramic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How was Esad Ramic appointed? I heard your answer but the court did not; could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies for repeating this, Esad Ramic was appointed by the ministry and the Territorial Defence staff in Sarajevo. I proposed him at the session of the war presidency of Konjic. In that meeting, the change took place, that is, Esad Ramic was supposed to take over the municipal staff and I was to take over the anti-aircraft defences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Redzepovic, were you appointed to member of the joint command of the TO and the HVO sometime in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the very beginning, we endeavoured to create a joint command together with the Croatian Defence Council and finally we succeeded in doing so in the month of May. We united both the commands and some units and we established a joint command and did what was needed in order to defend the joint territory. I was appointed the chief officer in charge of the anti-aircraft defences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While the joint command was operational, did you ever change your duties as the commander of the joint anti-aircraft defences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ever change my initial duties. From the start to the end, I remained the officer in charge of the anti-aircraft defences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any duties at that same time with the municipal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also did have a duty in the municipal staff; it was also to oversee the anti-aircraft defences. I was officer in charge of the anti-aircraft defences and also the commander of the anti-aircraft unit which was not a big unit, but at least it did have certain anti-aircraft weapons at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, while you were a member of the joint command and the municipal staff and not the commander, who issued you orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this military organisation, there were people who were authorised to issue orders and they were called commanders, so it had two stages, battalion and up and battalion and lower. The commander of the municipal headquarters was a person who issued orders to all officers in the headquarters and to all the units which were subordinate to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, a hypothetical question: If, in addition to a commander's signature on a document, there was a signature of a third person, what would be the significance of such a signature for you as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any such orders. If I saw one, maybe I could make a comment, but I cannot comment on it because I have not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Redzepovic, since you were the commander during the time when the Celebici barracks were controlled, at the time when you were commander, was there a decision adopted on the establishment of a prison in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was on this duty, the prison was not established, even though the barracks itself were taken control of during my position as commander. In other words, nobody established the prison while I was on duty, nor did I ever hear that somebody had established it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, did you meet Mr. Zejnil Delalic during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions, I saw him. I had not known him before that because I'm not from Konjic. I moved to Konjic in 1991 after the war in Croatia and I was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, as a commander and then as a member of the joint command and the headquarters staff, can you tell me whether Zejnil Delalic at any point in 1992 was a member of the joint command or the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic was never either a member of the municipal staff or any unit within the defence forces of the Konjic municipality. He had no duties there and also he could not be a member of our units or our headquarters because he was not on the mobilisation list or the wartime mobilisation list. People who were abroad, and he especially, he had been abroad for more than 20 years, he was not on the mobilisation list. He was not a soldier, so he could not have any duties in the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The court is aware of this. I'm not going to ask you whether Mr. Delalic was appointed coordinator at some point. As coordinator though, was Mr. Delalic superior to you, to your unit or to the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was the commander of my own unit, I never appointed Mr. Zejnil Delalic to a position of coordinator and he never showed me any accreditation or any document showing that he would be my superior officer so that we had no official relations of my being his commander or he being my commander during the period of time when I was a commander. Mr. Asim Dzambasevic was the person who was the representative of the high command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April when you first met him and before he went to Zagreb, did you know what his business was? What did he engage in, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I met Zejnil Delalic, those were very simple, short meetings at which I was only to state what we required in terms of equipment, food. It was made clear that he may be able to assist through his contacts and through his ability. We needed such assistance from different people given the situation in which we were and given the fact that we did not have any warehouses to rely on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, you are a person who was in charge of the anti-aircraft defences, so you were a field commander, not a staff commander. But was Mr. Delalic, if you know, ever appointed to a position of commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw a specific document, an order, but from my daily contacts with fellow officers, my colleagues, I do have information that in late July or early August he became commander of a tactical group, which is a fact that surprised me because I know that he was not a soldier and that he had no duties with our own staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether from this time, you said late July, early August, Mr. Zejnil Delalic as commander of the Tactical Group 1 was a superior officer to you or to the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a commander of Tactical Group, he could not have been superior to the municipal staff of Konjic, even though by orders of our own superior command, we had a duty to provide Tactical Group 1 with certain units, size of about 2 to 300 men. And in that way, that was all of our involvement with Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would this be a convenient moment to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How long do you intend to take with him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A short period, maybe 15 or 20 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him one question. When he became commander of all formations, was his unit also placed under the control? Ask him straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was your unit, the anti-aircraft unit, your light artillery, was it ever placed under the command of the Tactical Group 1 commander? In other words, was it subordinate to Zejnil Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My anti-aircraft unit was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You said you were asked by the supreme command to give him about 200 men of your own army. What is the relationship between your units and the TG-1 in respect of those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the relationship is concerned, the Tactical Group and all the units that were part of it is established by the superior command. At the same time, the superior command also issues orders to the subordinate commands, such as the municipal staff, to provide units, to provide a certain number of forces and join it to the Tactical Group 1. They are then subordinate to the commander of Tactical Group. As a municipal staff, we carried out the order of the supreme command in Sarajevo, and we set aside about 200 soldiers and officers as part of the Tactical Group 1. At that time, the commander of Tactical Group 1 was Mustafa Polutak, and this Tactical Group command had the right to use only those men who had joined the ranks of the Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please advise the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, before the break, their honours put some questions to you, so in that connection, I should like to make an additional question. Actually, you said that from among the units of the municipal staff, subordinated to Mustafa Polutak, 200 to 300 men were transferred under his command. I want to ask you, the remaining mobilised men, numbering 2 to 3,000 men, who were not subordinated to Mr. Polutak, under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations, according to the rules of combat and all other instructions regarding the separation of certain forces to join a tactical group, the superior command issues the appropriate order. Only those formation that come under the tactical group are under the command of the tactical group commander. The others, officers and men, who stayed behind in the area of Konjic, for instance, they remain under the command of the municipal staff of Territorial Defence of Konjic, which means that the tactical group has jurisdiction or the command over only those formations which have become a part of the tactical group. In this case, Tactical Group 1. The forces constituting the tactical group remain within that tactical group for as long as the need for this exists. Afterwards, they return to join their former units. After a task has been accomplished, the task for which the tactical group was indeed formed. So a tactical group is of a temporary nature and once it accomplishes its task, the units go back under the command of their former commanders and become an organic part of those former units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is, for me, an additional clarification from a professional. Mr. Redzepovic, since there is evidence before this Trial Chamber on the unit of Gajret that was subordinated to Mr. Polutak in the battle for Tinovo Brdo, tell me, after the failure of this first attempt to lift the blockade, the soldiers who participated in this operation and who returned to Konjic, under whose command were they placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were immediately placed under the command of the municipal staff because they actually belong to that command and those units of the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Redzepovic, where is the Tactical Group 1 based? Do you know where it was based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of daily reports, I know that it was based at Oranj, at Igman, at Pasaric. These were the bases and these command posts probably changed depending on needs and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzepovic, you have already told us that while you were the commander, there was no prison in the Celebici barracks. Tell me, do you know whether a part of the Celebici compound was, at a later stage, used to detain persons who participated in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the territory of Konjic Municipality, there was no prison of any kind. They didn't exist from the previous period, nor were they subsequently formed. Attached to the MUP, to the police, there is a room for detention, for interviewing people who may have done wrong or violated the law and where they can be held in detention up to 24 hours. We call this remand detention or a prison. This premise was big enough to hold four to five men. In view of the fact that there were captures during combat, captures of armed rebels in large numbers, they could not be placed in this detention of the police, but were placed in the Celebici barracks where there were facilities for the accommodation of personnel and where our own unit was housed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Redzepovic, after you ceased being a commander, did you ever visit the Celebici barracks? And my second question, did you ever visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told the Celebici barracks a couple of days later, after a special unit was accommodated there, a special combat unit, which was to be used for certain interventions --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When was this please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in April, end of April, perhaps. And a second time, when I was formerly sworn in, I don't remember exactly when that happened, but during the swearing in ceremony, it took place in Celebici. Those were the only times I visited Celebici. Because my duties were such that they did not involve visiting Celebici or seeking assistance there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what you have just told the court, are you personally aware if Zejnil Delalic had any kind of competence over the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that Zejnil Delalic was not even on the list for mobilisation. That he was not a soldier and that his role as commander came into being when he took over command of Tactical Group 1. I assume that he had no need to go to the Celebici barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that he had no authority over the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzepovic. Your Honours, I have completed my examination in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions. And again, I have managed to keep my notes on to one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, like you, I was in my army's air defence forces and so I am going to ask you some questions. About organisation, I think that from hearing your direct testimony, they were organised a lot like mine, but I want to make sure because it has something to do with the issues in this trial. After May, when you became the commander of the anti-aircraft forces and at the same time commander of the -- or, excuse me, staff officer for the anti-aircraft in the municipality, that's the time I want to focus on. And if I ask a question that's not clear, and sometimes I do that, please stop me and I'll clear it up for you, okay. Sir, while you were -- when you were in command of the anti-aircraft units, as a commander, did you have the right in our own name to issue orders to those troops on your own authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was a staff officer, that is when I -- my command duties were terminated according to the rules and regulations on which the military organisation is based. I was only able to prepare proposals to the commander regarding the execution of his orders, as a specialist for anti-aircraft defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you were basically the senior advisor on anti-aircraft for the commander of the municipal headquarters and his staff officer to aid him in doing that, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to aid the commander and the chief of staff, the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And while you were the officer, in your job as a staff officer, did you have the authority to issue orders on your own authority? Could you on your own authority issue orders to say the anti-tank troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I don't think your question is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'll tell you why, there must be certain type of orders which only the commander could issue. And there could be certain type of orders which to he had to issue to subordinate where to place his anti-aircraft guns, how to go about -- these are orders which he must be issuing himself on his own authority. It depends upon the nature of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, Judge Jan asked a good question. And let me come right to the heart of that. Besides being the staff officer, you had another job, didn't you, as the actual commander of the air defence units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concept of commander is something very important, very high up. I was lower than that. I was commander of a unit and the unit is a small sized unit, the size of a battery, and I was commander of that sized unit. It's not really a commander's duty but a chief of a group. As the chief of this unit, I could issue orders only to my anti-aircraft unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For instance, as Judge Jan has said, if you were given a mission to defend Celebici from air attack, you would have the authority to order those men in that unit to set up their weapons at various places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that was because of your role as the commander of the anti-aircraft unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could if I were to be given such an assignment. If Celebici were a facility of exceptional significance, then the anti-aircraft unit defends only those facilities and units which are of exceptional importance. It cannot defend everything, so the prison in Celebici and Celebici itself were not a defence facility of such importance for us to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I just made that as an example. But you would have the authority to position those troops, order them to take part in air defence because you were the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you had the authority as the commander of the anti-aircraft forces to punish troops who refused to obey orders or did other things that were wrong; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is because, and simply because, you were the commander as opposed to a deputy commander or a staff officer; is that not correct, sir? Sir, you have to say "yes" or "no." That lady over in front of us is called a court reporter and she has to write down everything we say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was the leader of a unit, I could command that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As a deputy commander or as a staff officer, you did not have the authority to command, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a staff officer, I could propose to the chief of staff or the commander certain measures and to participate in the drafting of his order for the use of the anti-aircraft units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, one thing you said after we came back from the break, you mentioned, and I may not have understood it when you were answering some questions from Ms. Residovic, you mentioned that there were other units on the Celebici barracks other than just the prison; did I understand that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. We didn't have such facilities. At the time, the army was in their houses, each individual in his own home, and according to the deployment plan, units would form and rally at a particular place, at a particular time. This was a great problem for us regarding the preservation of combat readiness of the units. That's why we badly needed a facility of a barracks type, like a barracks, where we would have a fully prepared unit for immediate engagement in the areas where the threat existed. In that sense, we sought to form the first units which would live the life of soldiers in barracks. The prison as such or a premise where prisoners were held occurred due to circumstances of the appearance of a large number of captured rebels who had, under arms, fought against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that at the time that the prison was operating at Celebici, there were also other units that were using and assigned to the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who was in overall command of the camp at the time, the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall with precision, but they were the leaders of units or commanders of units because there wasn't much space for accommodation. This was a small unit and they changed. They took turns in the barracks. For instance, if there was one company, the company leader would be the commander of the barracks. For the next seven days or fifteen days, another unit would be there and then the commander of that unit would be in command of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, the person who was in command of that company was the person who was in overall command of Celebici and the person who was in charge of overall security for Celebici; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Again, the question is not very clear. Apparently the Celebici facility was divided into two parts, one being used for the prison and the other for stationing of the troops. Your question is a person who was in charge of those troops which were stationed there was also in charge of the prison. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My question is someone in overall command of the entire facility, everything that is there, the prison and the troops that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was in two parts, the prison and a depot or a station for the troops. You ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You heard Judge Jan's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The judge is completely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was there somebody who was in charge of security for the entire camp or was that also divided into two different functions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Learned counsel means for the prison there was separate security or there was only one security arrangement for both portions of the Celebici set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me get right to the heart of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Separately, separately. There was separate security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There is a fence around the model. As you can see and as you know, there's a fence around the barracks. Who was in charge of securing that fence to make sure no one entered the prison or the barracks without permission? Was that a shared responsibility or did some one unit have responsibility to keep people out? If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure and I cannot answer this question. For a time, responsibility was shared. There was a special unit to provide security and another was combat-ready. In a different period of time, it was the same unit responsible both for the security of the barracks compound and for the unit itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the unit that was, for lack of a better phrase, the tenant unit, the unit that moved in and out, that unit would be responsible for the security of the large exterior perimeter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it was the same unit and sometimes other units that provided security. It wasn't always one in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that would be different from the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Esad Landzo has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions from the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have some questions, but because of the extremely late notice that this witness was going to be called today, we would be asking for some sort of recess for cross-examination and that we just proceed with the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can't you cross-examine on what he has said here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can start, but there's also additional research that we would like to do to try to find out additional information that may be relevant, and I would wish to have that information before me before I cross-examine. I believe that's, in fact, why we were supposed to get the order of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When, in fact, you are unable to get it, that doesn't mean you cannot make use of what answers have come out of the witness. We are getting a little too rigid about how to conduct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The only document he has referred to is his pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but it is often the case that there are additional documents that are relevant to a witness. If Your Honours wish me to start, I will start now, but we may be requesting additional time to do research and have the witness recalled. But if Your Honours direct me to start, I will certainly start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's better you start. I think you better learn how to take your witnesses as they come because there isn't much he could say which you might have not examined him from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, or good afternoon. My name is Theresa McHenry and I'm with the Prosecution and I will be asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you don't understand a question, sir, please just tell me that. I will also tell you, sir, that there are a number of questions, if not most of my questions, that all you have to do is answer "yes" or "no." So if you have already testified about something or you don't need to go over what you have stated again, then you don't need to explain your answer, unless you think a "yes" or "no" is somehow an unfair representation of the truth; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you would agree that because of the extraordinary circumstances in Konjic, a lot was going on, including with the military, that was not prescribed for in regulations or the structures that had originally been envisioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You speak very fast. Would you mind slowing down just a little?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. Sir, you would agree that, because of the extraordinary circumstances that Konjic found itself in, many things were happening in Konjic that were not as set out in regulations or the structures that had been envisioned by the regulations; would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree and you can never anticipate in a war what would happen. In other words, directions, regulations, you cannot set them out in advance because the war, as such, is a very complex thing. It was always possible that something unforeseen and unanticipated would occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Thus, you would agree that even until June of 1992, although the regulations prescribed that the war presidency was not supposed to have any involvement in the selection of the TO commander, in fact, the war presidency continued to nominate or select the TO commanders and, again, because of the extraordinary circumstances; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are two parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Nominate, Hadzihuseinovic said "Yes, we had done that with the commander." Appoint is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness responded twice to this question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer? The war presidency did not appoint. It only proposed or nominated, whereas the actual appointments were made by the command and presidency in Sarajevo. In other words, the war presidency in Konjic did not make appointments. The situation in Konjic as of April was such that the communications were not regular; here, I mean both the traffic, telecommunications, radio communications and all other communications. As early as April, Konjic was already under blockade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that because of the problems in communication, Konjic often had to take decisions and act independently of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In what fields? You see, you're referring to appointments. He has said no appointments were made by the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm just referring to in general, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In general, but a particular field, if you can. That would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You've been here all along, and both sides of the case, Prosecution and Defence, have been consistent in the way these matters were dealt with, whether it was sent to Sarajevo by courier, whether it came through some other devious means, they still sent to Sarajevo for confirmation. They did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case that with respect to various military matters, because of the communication difficulties, Konjic sometimes had to make decisions and act independently of Sarajevo; is that correct or not correct or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's too general. He has already said every authority in the war presidency and of the TO was acting within its own competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you specifically. It is the case that, pursuant to the regulations in May and June of 1992, the war presidency was not supposed to be even nominating commanders of the TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you don't know the answer to this question, you can say "I don't know," but my question, sir, is: You would agree that in May and June of 1992, under the regulations, the war presidency had no role in nominating commanders of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency took part in nomination, in proposals. I cannot remember exactly up until which date, but I think it may have been until May or June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you know in May and June of 1992 what the regulations about the authority of war presidencies were regarding the nomination of TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that in May and June of 1992, under the regulations, the war presidency had no role in nominating TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know from before that Konjic was under blockade and that the regulations or decrees with the force of law, the law on the defence forces which were adopted in May and June could not be implemented instantly in the territories which could not receive these new laws and regulations in a regular way. I cannot exactly tell you when it was that we received them, but I know that many of these regulations were passed in May and June. And the situation was such that the war presidency take the role of the authority which would nominate members of the TO staff for awhile longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, you would also agree with me that during this time when you were TO commander, you considered yourself part of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you previously give a statement in October of 1996 to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor referring to yourself and others as "we in the war presidency"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that that is what I said. In fact, I say that that is not how I put it, and I do not know why you are putting these words to me which I have never spoken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you also remember whether or not in your statement you specifically reported that the commander of the TO headquarters was a representative in the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the commander of the civilian protection, maybe this was mistranslated, but the commander of the civilian protection is a member of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during May -- let me move on. Sir, when was Mr. Dzambasevic present in Konjic approximately? .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the latter half of April, and I don't know when exactly he left Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But he could have left Konjic by the beginning part of May; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that could be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were the commander of the TO when the Celebici barracks were taken over; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the take-over of the barracks was a military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it a civilian operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not an operation. "Operation" imply much larger forces which are engaged in combat. There was no combat here; there was no use of weapons here. An agreement was reached and human lives were saved. These barracks had no significance for the aggressors either; so by mutual agreement, it was turned over peacefully to the officers of our Territorial Defence and to the representatives of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that Celebici had no military significance or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had no great significance. When you talk about significance, it could be tactical or strategic or operational. This was a depot which warehoused materiel. It had fuel and lubricants stored there. The position of Celebici was such that it wasn't strategically very important for the aggressor either. In that respect, they were glad to turn over the barracks, and here I mean by soldiers who had already completed their military duty. But the Belgrade regime had forced them to serve an additional three months as members of the reserve which was not what they did willingly. They were glad to be able to turn over the barracks without a fight and this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The weapons stored in Celebici, were they not of great military significance also? Sir, if you can just answer with a "yes" or "no" or "I don't know," please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons which were warehoused in Celebici were important for us because every rifle and every bullet was important for us. We did not enough of that and this is why it was important for us. But for the aggressors who had tanks and aircraft, this was not very significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that because of the extraordinary circumstances the decision to take over the Celebici barracks was made by both civilian and military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said a short while ago that both the forces of the Territorial Defence, that is, the officers, and the MUP forces and their commanders both took part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, did the civilian authorities have any involvement whatsoever in deciding or requesting that the barracks be taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any event, the coordination between the civilian, military and police authorities did exist; this was also necessary for a comprehensive preparation for the combat operations which were anticipated and which then took place in '92, '93 and '94. In any event, we did cooperate with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, what role did Mr. Delalic play, if any, in the take-over of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic did not take part in the take-over of the Celebici barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that he did not take any part whatsoever in the take-over of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not take any part, and I did not see him at all, nor have I heard of him being a participant of this action where the Celebici barracks were taken over from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you present, sir, when the barracks were taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not, but an operations officer went over there from my staff. His name is Midhat Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if Mr. Delalic was present during the take-over in any capacity whatsoever, you don't know anything about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand you that, as far as you know, Mr. Delalic was not present during the take-over of Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
